tldr: Instead of directly mimicking whole-body joint trajectories, this paper proposes a framework that uses contact planning—determining which body part contacts where in the environment and when—as an intermediary interface. This allows a single reinforcement learning policy to autonomously execute ladder climbing, wall scaling, jumping down, and fall recovery.
hero_caption: A single generalist policy enables the compact humanoid robot Unitree G1 to autonomously perform an extremely diverse range of whole-body mobility skills: climbing ladders, scaling walls, crawling through confined spaces, jumping down, and traversing stepping stones. It operates entirely from onboard sensors without using any reference trajectories at deployment to achieve adaptive contacts.
overview:
For humanoids to operate effectively in human environments, they must go beyond bipedal walking on flat ground. They need whole-body multi-contact mobility—such as climbing ladders, vaulting over obstacles, and crawling through tight spaces. However, learning this from scratch using pure reinforcement learning (RL) is difficult: the combinatorial space involving limbs and the torso is so vast that reward design and exploration alone struggle to elicit the desired whole-body coordination. On the other hand, methods that track reference motions (such as human motion capture) produce natural movements, but they have a major limitation: they cannot adapt to novel terrains that deviate even slightly from the training data.

The authors focused on an intuitive insight: when humans navigate rough terrain, they do not plan detailed joint trajectories for their entire body; instead, they unconsciously use vision to spot future contact locations (where to place a foot or grab a handhold). Rather than tracking full-body kinematic trajectories, what if contact—which body part touches where in the environment—is used as the intermediary representation (interface)? This abstraction could exploit natural whole-body coordination priors from motion data while preserving the flexible environmental adaptability of reinforcement learning.

The proposed framework introduces a three-stage learning pipeline combining an attention-based contact planner (which predicts future contact locations from LiDAR elevation maps and proprioception) and a contact-conditioned tracker (which achieves these contact targets). Extensive evaluations on real hardware (Unitree G1) and in simulation demonstrate that a single policy—without any reference inputs at deployment and relying solely on onboard sensors—achieves diverse and continuous whole-body behaviors, including ladder climbing, stepping stones, wall scaling, and even autonomous recovery from falls.
contributions: Established a control framework that uses contact plans across 9 body parts—rather than whole-body joint trajectories—as an intermediary interface, preventing overfitting to reference motions while acquiring natural whole-body coordination.
Developed a self-supervised Attention-based Contact Planner (ACP) that directly predicts appropriate contact points on an elevation map based on proprioception and goal commands.

Proposed a three-stage learning pipeline that bootstraps the planner and tracker together, bridging imitation learning to reinforcement learning fine-tuning on unseen, procedurally generated terrains.
Implemented an onboard LiDAR-based neural mapping method capable of reconstructing thin, protruding structures such as ladder rungs with high precision and low latency.

sections.heading: Stop mimicking trajectories: using contact as the interface
sections.summary: Conventional RL struggles to discover whole-body coordination due to vast exploration spaces, while motion imitation fails to adapt to unseen terrains. This paper proposes a new framework that unifies the benefits of both by replacing full-body trajectory tracking with contact location planning as the intermediary representation.
sections.details:
Navigating rough terrain and complex 3D obstacles requires humanoids to use multi-contact motions that engage the entire body—not just the feet, but also hands, knees, and the pelvis. However, solving this with pure reinforcement learning presents a combinatorial explosion: deciding which body part to place, where, and when. Minor differences in reward weights drastically alter robot behavior, leading to tedious trial-and-error engineering.

On the other hand, imitation learning—retargeting human motion data to a robot and tracking it—readily produces natural, coordinated motions. Yet it remains bound to predefined reference trajectories and breaks down as soon as the robot encounters unfamiliar terrain. Furthermore, generating or modifying trajectories online is extremely costly when trying to produce dynamically feasible full-body motions with intermittent contact.

Here, the authors posed a fundamental question: does a robot really need to copy complete joint trajectories to learn whole-body mobility? When humans traverse rugged environments, vision scouts the next footholds and handholds. The crucial element is where environmental interactions (contacts) occur; the intermediate joint motions connecting those contact points have numerous degrees of freedom.

Therefore, this work extracts only the contact structure from reference motion data, using it as the interface between perception and control. A contact planner predicts future contact locations from an elevation map, and a tracker policy moves the body to realize those contacts through reinforcement learning. This eliminates all reference trajectories at deployment, yielding a single generalist policy that operates purely on onboard sensing and goal commands.

sections.heading: From ladder climbing to stepping stones and fall recovery: broad versatility on hardware and in simulation
sections.summary: Using the real Unitree G1 robot, the framework demonstrated diverse skills including ladder climbing, wall scaling, crawling, jumping down, and autonomous fall recovery. In simulation, it achieved a 92.5% success rate on complex composite terrains, substantially outperforming a diffusion-based trajectory generation baseline (58.8%).
sections.details:
### 0.1 Agile, versatile whole-body mobility and goal-conditioned behavior branching
In hardware experiments on the Unitree G1, a single policy traversed varied obstacles using onboard sensors alone. Notably, given the exact same terrain, completely different behaviors emerged autonomously depending on user-specified goal commands (target position and heading).
For instance, facing the same box, the robot simply steps up onto it if the goal is low, but uses its hands to climb up if the goal is high. If the goal faces backward, it sits down; if the goal points sideways, it turns its body and scales the obstacle laterally. Furthermore, after climbing up, if the goal lies deep inside a low-clearance passage, it crouches down to crawl and then stands up afterwards. These behavioral transitions connect smoothly without any manual state machine.

### 0.2 Self-righting recovery from unexpected falls
Real-world environments inevitably involve perceptual noise and slippery footholds, yet the policy showed strong robustness and emergent failure recovery. When the robot stumbled while landing after jumping down, or when its knee caught on a rung and slipped while climbing a ladder, it autonomously recovered its posture, stood back up, and resumed locomotion as if nothing had happened. These recovery behaviors were not present in the original motion capture data; they were discovered autonomously through reinforcement learning exploration.

### 0.3 Quantitative simulation evaluations and ablations
Simulation experiments thoroughly evaluated performance across three terrain categories: terrains with reference motions, procedurally generated terrains for fine-tuning, and completely unseen composite terrains.

- Input to the tracker: Adding full-body kinematic details (such as joint trajectories) did not improve success rates; contact location targets alone were entirely sufficient (over 98.5% success rate).
- Planner architecture: Comparing a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with an attention mechanism showed that attention was clearly superior on sparse terrains with discrete footholds and in environments with perceptual noise or irrelevant obstacles. This stems from its ability to selectively attend to where feet should be placed on the elevation map.
- Effect of RL fine-tuning: Passing through Stage 3 RL boosted the success rate on sparse whole-body contact terrains by 54.8 percentage points and drastically lowered contact positioning error.

In comparisons with MGMT, a state-of-the-art diffusion-based trajectory generator, the proposed method outperformed it across all 11 evaluated categories. The margin was especially pronounced in environments demanding precise contact placement, such as stepping stones and ladders. Across 8 demanding composite courses, the proposed method attained an average success rate of 92.5%, compared to 58.8% for MGMT. While MGMT occasionally generated physically impossible trajectories that reached into empty air, the proposed approach constrains contact points to actual surfaces on the elevation map, ensuring reliable support bases.

sections.heading: The essence of whole-body mobility is a sequence of contacts
sections.summary: This study shows that contact-centric abstraction provides an effective control interface for humanoids. However, the system currently relies on 2.5D elevation maps, leaving challenges for overhead hanging motions and semantic global navigation.
sections.details:
The key insight of this work is that using contact—a physical interaction—as the control interface harmoniously merges the natural coordination found in large motion datasets with the environmental adaptability and robustness of reinforcement learning. Instead of constraining full joint trajectories, providing only essential contact constraints allows the policy to flexibly shape limb trajectories according to the contours of the terrain.

Furthermore, designing the attention mechanism to select which environmental points to contact based on body state and goal commands provides rich expressive capacity, eliciting different behaviors from the same terrain depending on intent. Walking, climbing, crawling, and fall recovery can all be described under a single unified lens: differences in contact sequences between the body and the environment.

Three main limitations remain:
First, perception and contact planning currently rely on 2.5D elevation maps. This setup cannot support full 3D contacts, such as hanging from monkey bars overhead or bracing hands against a tunnel ceiling.
Second, the system is designed for local locomotion toward goals a few meters away; semantic reasoning and global navigation across entire buildings are outside its current scope.
Third, acrobatic movements that share identical contact sequences over short horizons but feature radically different airborne full-body dynamics—such as a backflip versus a vertical jump, where both merely push off and land—cannot be distinguished by contact targets alone and remain difficult to handle within this framework.

sections.heading: Under the hood: the three-stage training pipeline and LiDAR neural mapping
sections.summary: The authors built a three-stage pipeline: contact-annotated retargeting from human motion, contact-conditioned tracker training, an attention-based contact planner, and RL fine-tuning on novel terrains. They also developed a LiDAR mapping pipeline that accurately captures thin ladder rungs.
sections.details:
### Motion retargeting and contact extraction
Directly transferring human motion capture data to robot joint angles causes joint limit violations and foot-ground penetration. By solving nonlinear inverse kinematics (IK) to avoid geometric penetrations, the system automatically extracted the timing and 3D locations of contacts across 9 body parts: both feet, both knees, both hands, both elbows, and the pelvis.

### Contact-conditioned tracker (Stage 1)
The tracker is a 3-layer MLP (hidden dimensions 512-256-128) that takes the past 5 steps of proprioception, a local elevation map ($9\times 7$ points), target contact coordinates for the 9 body parts, and the goal command. It outputs 23-DoF joint position offsets at 50 Hz. Initially, ground-truth contact locations from reference data serve as an oracle. Using Curriculum State Initialization (CSI), where rollout starting points gradually move earlier from the end of a motion, the tracker learns coordinated whole-body control that reliably reaches contact targets.

### Attention-based contact planner (Stage 2)
The planner inspects the elevation map ($17\times 11=187$ points) based on proprioception and goal commands to select future contact locations (within 1.5 seconds). It employs multi-head attention (32 heads, 96 dimensions) where queries—modulated per body part via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM)—query the key/value features of map points. Crucially, the model does not directly regress continuous 3D coordinates in space; instead, it predicts affordance probability distributions over observed surface points. This fundamentally prevents the planner from predicting nonsensical locations in mid-air. Training data is generated via Hindsight Contact Labeling, extracting successful contacts from previous tracker rollouts.

### Reinforcement learning fine-tuning (Stage 3)
The tracker executes contact targets proposed by the planner, and successful trials are added to the planner's replay buffer, mutually improving both components. Procedurally generated environments without motion references—such as randomized steps, stepping stones, gaps, and inclined ladders—are introduced. Fine-tuning uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with goal-reaching and contact-tracking rewards. To prevent catastrophic forgetting of base motions, the policy samples from the original dataset and novel terrains in parallel.

### LiDAR neural mapping
Point clouds from a Livox MID-360 LiDAR mounted on the head are projected onto a 2.5D grid (3 cm resolution). A CNN predicts one of three correction modes for each grid cell—adopt raw measurement, adopt neighborhood mean, or discard as empty—along with an uncertainty estimate. To prevent protruding structures like ladder rungs from being overwritten by scans of the floor underneath, a line-of-sight geometric heuristic is integrated into the fusion step. The entire mapping pipeline runs within 30 ms on an onboard Jetson Orin NX.

sections.heading: Appendix: fine-grained design and curricula for stable training
sections.summary: This section covers reward function details, domain randomization parameters, the asymmetric actor-critic setup in PPO, and concrete curriculum parameters for gradual difficulty progression.
sections.details:
### Asymmetric actor-critic and dual critics
To stabilize training, the actor (policy) receives only observations available on the real robot: noisy proprioceptive history, local elevation map, goal command, and predicted contact targets. The critic (value function), meanwhile, receives privileged simulation information such as true base velocity and external disturbance parameters. In Stage 3, two independent critic networks are maintained—one for the reference motion environment ($V_m$) and one for the free exploration environment ($V_{\mathrm{fs}}$)—preventing interference between disparate reward scales.

### Contact and reward annealing schedules
In Stage 2, the contact input to the tracker is probabilistically transitioned from ground-truth reference contacts to predicted contacts from the planner. The schedule for switching the input observation ($\eta_{\mathrm{obs}}$) precedes the schedule for switching the reward weight ($\eta_{\mathrm{rew}}$). Familiarizing the tracker with planner predictions before rewarding it for tracking them prevents policy collapse.

### Terrain difficulty curriculum
For procedurally generated terrains in Stage 3, obstacle parameters—such as step heights, gap widths, and spacing between footholds—are organized into 10 discrete difficulty levels. If the smoothed success rate (reaching within 0.5 m of the goal without falling) exceeds 50%, the robot advances to a higher level; persistent failures lead to demotion. This automated curriculum allows the robot to adapt smoothly to challenging full-body climbing and gap-crossing maneuvers.

takeaways: Using contact points (where and when to make contact) as an abstracted interface—rather than directly learning full-body joint trajectories—dramatically improves exploration efficiency and adaptability in high-DoF humanoids.

Formulating contact prediction as attention (affordance distribution) over observed surface geometry (elevation maps), rather than continuous 3D coordinate regression, prevents contacts from landing in empty air and guarantees high geometric accuracy.
Motion capture demonstrations are most effective when treated not as rigid trajectories to track, but as prior distributions over contact patterns to guide reinforcement learning exploration.
limitations: Relying on 2.5D elevation maps prevents the system from directly interacting with full 3D geometry, such as hanging from overhead monkey bars or bracing hands against a ceiling.

Behaviors with identical contact sequences over short intervals (e.g., a vertical jump vs. a backflip, which share identical takeoff and landing contacts but have entirely different airborne motions) cannot be uniquely specified or controlled via contact targets alone.
The policy is specialized for local locomotion toward goals a few meters away; integrating semantic scene understanding for long-range, building-scale navigation remains future work.
